title: Cross-Platform Test Automation: Web, iOS + Android in One Suite
summary: One testing platform for your web app and iOS/Android apps: a single plain-English test format, hosted browsers, emulators and simulators, parallel runs.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- **Momentic** uses one plain-English test format across web, iOS, and Android. It runs tests on hosted browsers, emulators, and simulators.
- **BrowserStack** provides browser and real-device infrastructure for existing test suites. It does not replace separate authoring frameworks.
- **LambdaTest** provides browser and device infrastructure with parallel orchestration. You still maintain separate frameworks for each surface.
- **mabl** covers web and API testing. Native iOS and Android apps require another tool.
- **Appium** provides code-first native mobile automation without a built-in device cloud or unified web test layer.


## Why testing web and mobile separately is becoming a maintenance problem


Separate web and mobile suites turn one product change into repeated test maintenance. You may encode a checkout flow in Playwright for the web, then recreate the same behavior in Appium for mobile. Teams using native frameworks maintain additional XCUITest and Espresso code. Each framework brings its own locators, runner configuration, and failure output.


Mobile coverage must account for active OS versions, screen sizes, display densities, network conditions, and hardware-specific behavior.


A shared UI change exposes the maintenance failure mode. When a commit renames a button or changes a navigation path, engineers must update Playwright locators and then reproduce the fix in each mobile framework. Delayed updates leave stale tests, while missed updates create coverage gaps.


Failures also arrive through separate CI jobs and reports. Engineers must determine whether each failure represents a regression, a stale selector, or a device-specific issue using evidence produced by different runners. As web and native apps change together, duplicated authoring and triage consume time that could otherwise expand meaningful coverage.


## What "one suite" actually requires


A cross-platform suite needs one authoring format that expresses tests across web, native iOS, and native Android. It also needs hosted execution environments and parallel runs across those targets. The authoring format should avoid separate Playwright, Appium, or XCUITest implementations for shared flows. The runner should provide hosted browsers and mobile emulators or simulators, then execute the targets concurrently so each additional target does not add its full runtime to the CI/CD job.


A device cloud meets a different need. Services such as BrowserStack and LambdaTest run suites written with frameworks such as Selenium, Playwright, Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest. Their device infrastructure does not by itself provide one test definition across web and native apps. Real-device access therefore does not prove that a tool offers one authoring format. The comparison below credits real-device farms only when the available research supports that claim.


### Momentic


Momentic gives engineers one plain-English test format for web, iOS, and Android. Momentic applies one authored flow across hosted browsers, Android emulators, and iOS simulators when the product behavior is equivalent on each surface. Engineers avoid rewriting the same behavior in Playwright for web and Appium or XCUITest for mobile.


Momentic applies one authored test to multiple execution targets in the same run. CI/CD pipelines can trigger those targets on commits or deploys, and parallel execution reduces the time spent waiting for browser and mobile runs to finish sequentially. Engineers still need platform-specific tests when native behavior differs, but shared flows no longer require separate framework implementations.


Visual checks use the same assertion format across browsers, emulators, and simulators, while each target renders its own interface. Before adopting the feature, verify how Momentic stores target-specific baselines, handles rendering variation, and configures comparison tolerances. Link these claims to Momentic documentation before publication.


Momentic currently covers hosted browsers and emulators or simulators. It should not be treated as a real-device farm. Teams that need verification against physical device hardware, manufacturer-specific Android builds, or device sensors may still need BrowserStack, LambdaTest, or another device cloud.


**Pros.** One test format avoids separate implementations of shared flows in Playwright and Appium or XCUITest. Parallel execution can return browser and mobile results in the same CI/CD run instead of waiting for each target sequentially.


**Cons.** Emulator and simulator coverage cannot replace every physical-device test. Teams may also retain Playwright, Appium, or XCUITest for low-level cases that require framework-specific APIs or hardware access.


**Pricing.** Current pricing was not provided in the supplied research. Check[Momentic](https://momentic.ai/) for available plans and commercial terms.


### BrowserStack


BrowserStack fits teams that already maintain separate web and mobile test suites but do not want to operate device infrastructure. It provides hosted browsers and broad real-device access for existing Selenium, Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest suites.


BrowserStack separates interactive testing in[App Live](https://www.browserstack.com/app-live) from automated suite execution in[App Automate](https://www.browserstack.com/app-automate) . BrowserStack manages device availability and test execution. Your CI/CD pipeline still supplies the test code and invokes the appropriate framework.


BrowserStack does not provide one authoring format across web, iOS, and Android. Its device cloud does not eliminate the need to author and maintain the underlying Selenium, Playwright, Appium, Espresso, or XCUITest suites. A UI change may still require updates in Selenium or Playwright for web and Appium, Espresso, or XCUITest for mobile.


Choose BrowserStack when real-device coverage is the requirement and your existing suites already produce useful signal. Teams seeking one test definition across all three surfaces will still need an authoring and maintenance layer above BrowserStack.


### LambdaTest


LambdaTest puts browser infrastructure, real mobile devices, and execution orchestration under one vendor, but it does not remove the framework split between web and native apps. Web suites typically use Selenium or another browser framework. Native iOS and Android suites still use Appium, Espresso, or XCUITest.


LambdaTest offers web and API testing alongside real-device access in the same platform. HyperExecute provides parallel orchestration for those jobs, while LambdaTest supplies the execution environments. LambdaTest's mobile execution layer runs suites written with supported frameworks rather than introducing one authoring format shared by browser and native-app tests.


LambdaTest fits teams that want one vendor relationship and dashboard for browser and device infrastructure. You still maintain separate test codebases, selectors, dependencies, and framework upgrades for each surface. If your goal is one test definition that runs unchanged across web, iOS, and Android, LambdaTest alone does not provide that authoring model.


### mabl


mabl fits teams that want low-code test creation for browser and API coverage. Its web tooling includes locator-recovery and visual-comparison features. Link both capabilities to current mabl documentation before publication, and verify that mabl's current native-mobile scope has not changed. Those capabilities can reduce maintenance within a browser test suite.


mabl does not provide native iOS or Android app testing. Testing a responsive site in a mobile browser still exercises the web application, not native views, platform APIs, or installed app behavior.


A team shipping native apps would need Appium or another mobile app testing tool alongside mabl. Separate tooling brings back the test definitions, CI/CD configuration, and failure triage that a unified suite should consolidate. For the specific requirement of one test format across web, iOS, and Android, mabl does not qualify.


### Appium


Appium gives engineers code-level control over native, hybrid, and mobile browser tests on iOS and Android. Its server accepts WebDriver commands and passes them to platform drivers such as XCUITest for iOS and UiAutomator2 for Android.


[Appium](https://appium.io/docs/en/latest/intro/) is an automation framework rather than a hosted device cloud. You run its tests on local devices, emulators, simulators, private labs, or third-party clouds such as BrowserStack and LambdaTest. Appium's primary scope is app automation through platform drivers. A cross-platform suite that also targets hosted desktop browsers generally uses a browser framework such as Playwright or Selenium for that surface.


Appium leaves test authoring and maintenance to your engineering team. You own the code, selectors, CI/CD configuration, retries, and flaky-test investigation. Appium does not provide a unified authoring format or built-in tooling that maintains tests across web, iOS, and Android.


Appium fits teams with existing native test infrastructure and enough in-house capacity to maintain it. Choose it when deep platform control matters more than consolidating web and mobile verification into one suite.


## Comparison table


The relevant distinction is whether a product supplies execution infrastructure, a shared authoring format, or both. The table compares each product against the requirement of one test definition across web, iOS, and Android.

## How this replaces maintaining Playwright and Appium side by side


A unified test format removes duplicate framework work when the same user journey exists on web, iOS, and Android. With Playwright and Appium or XCUITest side by side, engineers encode that journey in separate APIs and maintain different element-location strategies. A plain-English test defines the expected behavior once, while the runner handles interactions for each target surface.


A hosted cross-platform runner can also reduce CI/CD provisioning. Separate suites often require Playwright browser dependencies, Appium drivers, mobile SDKs, and dedicated runner configuration. Hosted browsers, emulators, and simulators let one CI job trigger the cross-platform suite without provisioning each execution environment independently. Parallel execution can then run the same check against each target without separate pipeline definitions.


Failure investigation becomes less fragmented because engineers no longer triage equivalent scenarios across unrelated test runners. Separate frameworks produce different logs, retry behavior, and failure conventions. A shared execution layer places web and native results in one report. Engineers can compare the evidence for equivalent flows without switching among unrelated runners.


Consolidation does not remove real differences between a DOM and a native accessibility tree. Platform-specific permissions, navigation, and controls may still require conditional steps. The unified format removes duplicated framework plumbing while preserving those necessary branches.


Each additional test codebase creates another implementation that engineers must update when shared product behavior changes. One format reduces the number of suites that require selector updates, CI maintenance, and flaky-test investigation after each product change.


## FAQs


**What is the difference between mobile web testing and native app testing?**


Mobile web testing exercises a site inside mobile browsers and catches differences among rendering engines, responsive layouts, and browser behavior. Native app testing drives an installed iOS or Android binary and covers OS permissions, gestures, notifications, and hardware integrations that browser tests cannot reach. A complete test plan therefore treats mobile-browser behavior and installed-app behavior as separate coverage areas.


**Are emulators and simulators sufficient for mobile app testing?**


Emulators and simulators provide fast feedback for CI/CD, smoke tests, and parallel regression runs. Use real devices when a test depends on physical hardware, manufacturer-specific Android behavior, production performance characteristics, or an integration that the selected virtual device cannot reproduce faithfully. Virtual devices can handle frequent CI/CD checks, while targeted real-device runs cover those remaining cases.


**Can a unified suite coexist with Playwright and Appium during migration?**


Yes. You can add unified tests to the existing CI/CD pipeline while Playwright and Appium continue covering flows that have not moved. Migrate one product journey at a time, compare failure evidence, and remove the older test only after the replacement covers the same behavior.


**How does visual regression testing differ across browsers, emulators, and simulators?**


Browsers can render the same page differently because Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox use different rendering engines. Android emulators and iOS simulators add platform fonts, controls, screen densities, and OS rendering behavior. Visual checks should therefore compare each target against an environment-specific baseline rather than treating one image as canonical across web, iOS, and Android.


## Choosing a test suite for your stack


Choose based on the test infrastructure you maintain today. If the same engineering group owns web, iOS, and Android flows, evaluate whether one authoring format, hosted browsers, virtual mobile devices, and parallel execution would remove duplicated implementation work. A vendor that provides devices without a shared authoring layer leaves you maintaining separate Playwright and Appium suites.


Keep existing frameworks when they provide needed platform control and their maintenance cost remains acceptable. Consolidation becomes useful when duplicated selectors, CI/CD configuration, and flaky-test triage consume engineering time or leave coverage gaps across surfaces.


If a unified format matches your requirements,[sign up for Momentic](https://momentic.ai/) and run one representative flow on web, iOS, and Android before migrating the broader suite.
